policy_title: Reform Taxation of International Flights and Introduce Private Jet Super Tax
stated: Reduce the climate impact of flying by: Reforming the taxation of international flights to focus on those who fly the most, while reducing costs for ordinary households. Introducing a new super tax on private jet flights, and removing the VAT exemptions for private, first-class and business-class flights. Banning short domestic flights where a direct rail option taking less than 2.5 hours is available for the same journey, unless planes are alternative-fuelled.

source.quote: Reduce the climate impact of flying by: Reforming the taxation of international flights to focus on those who fly the most, while reducing costs for ordinary households who take one or two international return flights per year. Introducing a new super tax on private jet flights, and removing the VAT exemptions for private, first-class and business-class flights. Banning short domestic flights where a direct rail option taking less than 2.5 hours is available for the same journey, unless planes are alternative-fuelled.

bearing_set.reason: The policy's explicit aim is to reduce aviation's climate impact via flight-tax reform, private-jet super tax, VAT removal on premium fares, and a domestic short-haul ban where rail alternatives exist — all of which directly bear on the UK's emissions trajectory, a core O6 indicator.

The stated redesign explicitly shifts the tax burden from infrequent to frequent flyers to 'reduce costs for ordinary households', giving a concrete mechanism that would move real disposable income and the travel-cost component of the inflation basket for lower-frequency fliers; the domestic flight ban also has a plausible countervailing effect on travel costs (rail substitution) for those households.

Reforming international flight taxation to favour infrequent (ordinary) flyers reduces their tax burden on flights, while raising it sharply for frequent flyers and private/first/business-class passengers — a real, non-trivial shift in the household tax burden by travel intensity.

The policy explicitly redistributes aviation tax from ordinary/occasional flyers to wealthy frequent flyers and private jet users, narrowing the distributional gap in who bears the cost of aviation's externalities.

A domestic-flight ban (even qualified by the 2.5-hr rail threshold) removes connectivity options for business travel on affected routes, and the private-jet/business-class tax increases raise costs for commercial activity that relies on premium aviation — real but constrained by the qualifying rail condition.

membership_note: Core bearings are the environmental redesign (O6), the redistribution of aviation tax burden (O11 and O14 as distinct effects), and the productivity/connectivity cost of removing some domestic routes (O13). Flying is not an O2-essential; the fiscal revenue effects on O12 are plausible but too uncertain in magnitude without cost estimates to clear the non-negligible bar.
